Your perception surprises you

The triangle that is not there: Kanizsa

Three circles with a wedge cut out are enough for us to see a white triangle with sharp edges.

In 1955, the Italian psychologist Gaetano Kanizsa published a famous figure: three black circles, each with a wedge cut out, arranged so that the gaps face each other. We see a white triangle that looks brighter than the background and has clear edges. But no edge is drawn.

Illusory contours

These are called illusory or subjective contours. The brain prefers the simplest interpretation: it is more likely that a triangle is covering three circles than that three notched circles happen to line up by chance. It is an example of Gestalt principles such as closure.

In 1984 it was found that some neurons in the visual cortex of monkeys respond to these non-existent edges just as they do to real ones. The illusion is not just a later interpretation: the visual system builds the contour at early stages of processing.

References

  1. Kanizsa, G. (1955). Margini quasi-percettivi in campi con stimolazione omogenea. Rivista di Psicologia, 49(1), 7–30.
  2. von der Heydt, R., Peterhans, E. y Baumgartner, G. (1984). Illusory contours and cortical neuron responses. Science, 224(4654), 1260–1262.
